catalog_quote: Part of the language’s morphemes feature stress as one of their permanent phonological properties. Morphemes that feature stress are almost always stressed (but see below for cases of stressed morphemes that may be left unstressed in discourse), while morphemes that do not feature stress never are. Whether a morpheme belongs to the category of stressed morphemes or unstressed morphemes is not a lexical property, but rather depends on the nature of that morpheme; this distribution is explained below. The position of stress within a stressed morpheme is determined automatically and is absolutely fixed. Stressed morphemes always bear stress on their first syllable. Consequently, stress position cannot create contrasts between morphemes. The first syllable of independent morphemes—i.e. morphemes that may be uttered on their own, including in particular verbs and independent nouns—is regularly stressed, as in examples (33a–33f). The main phonological function of stress is therefore not a contrastive one, but a demarcative one: stress signals the beginning of independent morphemes. ... By contrast, dependent morphemes—i.e. morphemes that need to associate with some other morpheme to appear in discourse, and more specifically clitics and most bound morphemes—are entirely unstressed, as in (34a–86e). A prosodic word may only contain a single stressed morpheme—and must contain one—while it may in principle contain any number of unstressed morphemes, including none.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Ticuna (ticu1245) is not in the catalog. Of the four title-works with stress in the title: (1) Rodrigues & Martins 1999 'vogais acentuadas de Braga' is a European Portuguese (Braga) acoustic study, mis-assigned to Ticuna by Glottolog's own 'computerized assignment from acustico' -- irrelevant, priority none. (2) Soares 1996 (Letras de Hoje 31(2): 7-26; real title 'Regulação rítmica e ATUAÇÃO do OCP em Tikuna') was found open on the PUCRS OJS site, downloaded (scan, no text; scanned with tesseract at 300 dpi and checked against the page scan) and. p. 21 states that a rule makes the leftmost syllable of a root the stress bearer, stress being interpreted as long duration. (3) Soares 2000 (Editora da UNICAMP book, Vol. I = syntax) not located online; print only, low priority because it is the book edition of (4). (4) Soares 1992 UNICAMP thesis was already held by the project (etnolinguistica.org scan with text; official copy also at DOI 10.47749/t/unicamp.1992.46445) and read: Vol. II p. 607 'A sílaba mais à esquerda de uma raiz é portadora de acento', with the consequence (p. 616) that stress is usually penultimate since roots are mostly disyllabic, antepenultimate in monosyllable+disyllable compounds, and monosyllabic content words are stressed/long. Best first-hand statement read: Skilton 2023 PDA §4 p. 15 (fixed initial stress on the Prosodic Word = root-initial for most classes, duration the primary correlate, with measurements), converging with Soares 1992/1996 and Bertet 2020 pp. 83-85 (stressed morphemes always stressed on their first syllable; demarcative). searches were done by automated download/direct download against the journal archive, Glottolog, Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and Open Library.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ticuna is a tone language (10 tonemes in stressed syllables, 6 in unstressed per Bertet; 5 level tones per Skilton) that also has non-contrastive, demarcative word stress fixed on the first syllable of the lexical root / independent morpheme (= first syllable of the prosodic word); proclitics precede it unstressed, suffixes/enclitics/bound nouns follow it unstressed; one stress per prosodic word; main correlate is vowel duration. Skilton 2023 (Cushillococha, Peru: 'stress always falls on the first syllable of the PrWd', p.19) and Soares 1992/2020 (Brazil: 'localizado na sílaba mais à esquerda de uma raiz') state the same rule independently.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Bertet: none described (a prosodic word has exactly one stressed syllable). Skilton 2023: no evidence for iterative footing beyond the initial foot. Soares 1992/2020: posits an additional 'acento rítmico' (rhythmic stress, realized as a second long duration) that can appear on suffix strings away from the root stress, built right-to-left in binary feet.
new_statements.exceptions: Bertet: a few dependent morphemes (personal roots, deictic roots, first part of the bipartite deictic verb) are regularly stressed; a few independent function words ('my', 'and', prf) are usually left unstressed in discourse, in which case stress is dropped, never shifted; pre-pausal stressed short vowels are not lengthened. Skilton: inalienable nouns (second member of compounds) never stressed; loanwords may show stress-licensed segments in non-initial syllables.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the prosodic word = one independent (root) morpheme plus any clitics/affixes; stress is root-initial, hence not necessarily initial in the orthographic/cliticized word (subject proclitics precede the stress). Statements based on both elicited citation forms and spontaneous texts; Skilton adds duration measurements.
new_statements.identity_note: Three first-hand descriptions of three national varieties agree: Bertet 2020 describes the San Martín de Amacayacu variety (Colombia, 'smat'); Skilton 2023 the Cushillococha variety (Peru); Soares 1992/2020 Brazilian Tikuna (upper Solimões). Glottolog treats Ticuna as a single language ticu1245 with no dialect glottocodes; all three describe the same root-/prosodic-word-initial stress in a language with a large tone inventory (5 level tones per Skilton/Anderson; 10 tonemes in stressed syllables per Bertet).

new_statements.quote: Stress in Cushillococha Ticuna is fixed on the initial syllable of the Prosodic Word, which is – for most word classes – the initial syllable of the root (§4.1-4.6). The primary acoustic correlate of stress is duration (§4.7). Phonological consequences of stress are far-reaching, affecting contrast licensing (§5), lexical phonology (§§6-7), and grammatical tone (§8). Other research on varieties of Ticuna describes different stress-tone interactions. For the Cushillococha variety, L. Anderson (1959) and D. Anderson (1962) do not recognize the existence of stress.
new_statements.citation: Skilton, Amalia. 2023. Tone, stress, and their interactions in Cushillococha Ticuna. Phonological Data and Analysis 5(5): 1-44. doi:10.3765/pda.v5art5.58 (CC BY). [Not a title-works with stress in the title; already held by the project from the earlier reading and read in this search of works with stress in the title. Converges with Soares 1992 p. 607 / 1996 p. 21 and Bertet 2020 pp. 83-85, which are this search of works with stress in the title's own statements.]
new_statements.reading: Fixed root/prosodic-word-initial stress (proclitics never stressed; in compounds/inalienable possession only the first stem is stressed), cued primarily by vowel duration (stressed ~159-201 ms vs unstressed ~123 ms), in a language with five (Skilton) to ten/sixteen (Bertet) tonemes. Three independent first-hand descriptions agree: Soares 1992/1996 (Brazilian varieties: leftmost syllable of the root bears stress, realised as length; hence usually penultimate because roots are mostly disyllabic, antepenultimate in monosyllable+disyllable compounds), Bertet 2020 pp. 83-85 (San Martín de Amacayacu, Colombia: stressed morphemes always bear stress on their first syllable; demarcative; duration the main correlate), and Skilton 2023 (Cushillococha, Peru). A catalog entry would be: fixed initial (root-initial) stress, non-contrastive, duration-cued, coexisting with lexical tone; the older SIL descriptions (Anderson 1959/1962) and the Stanford Phonology Archive report no stress information.

tone_statements.citation: Alberto, Osias Guedes. 2021. Análise da adaptação fonológica e prosódica de empréstimos lexicais da língua portuguesa na língua tikuna [Analysis of phonology and prosodic adaptation of Portuguese language lexical loans in the Tikuna language]. Dissertação (Mestrado em Linguística), Instituto de Estudos da Linguagem, Universidade Estadual de Campinas, Campinas. 66 pp. (orient. Maria Filomena Spatti Sândalo; banca: Angel H. Corbera Mori, Marília Facó Soares).
tone_statements.quote: Para este objetivo, nesta investigação, seguiremos a análise de Montes (1995). No seu estudo, a autora explica que o tom fonológico apresenta três níveis de alturas possíveis, com presença de alofonias gerando cinco níveis de alturas fonéticas. O tikuna, portanto, é uma língua tonal enquanto o português não é. … quando os itens lexicais provenientes do PB entram no tikuna , recebem um contorno tonal, que será sempre médio (M), médio (M), baixo (B), o que no final das contas gera uma nova gramática, uma vez que nas palavras originais tikuna, qual tom ocorre em cada sílaba é imprevisível.
tone_statements.translation: For this purpose, in this investigation, we follow the analysis of Montes (1995). In her study the author explains that phonological tone has three possible pitch levels, with allophony producing five phonetic pitch levels. Tikuna is therefore a tone language whereas Portuguese is not. … when lexical items from Brazilian Portuguese enter Tikuna, they receive a tonal contour which is always mid (M), mid (M), low (B), which in the end creates a new grammar, since in native Tikuna words which tone occurs on each syllable is unpredictable.
tone_statements.locator: p. 55, Cap. IV '4. O sistema tonal da língua tikuna' and '4.1 O acento do português para o tom no tikuna'; level names alto/médio/baixo at 1.5.5 Montes, p. 26
tone_statements.summary: Tone language: after Montes (1995), three phonological levels (high, mid, low), five phonetic by allophony; native tone unpredictable per syllable; Portuguese loans take a fixed M..M-L contour.

tone_statements.citation: Felix, Nazareno Sampaio. 2018. Do texto à melodia das palavras na língua Ticuna. Dissertação (Mestrado Profissional em Linguística e Línguas Indígenas), Museu Nacional, Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro, Rio de Janeiro.
tone_statements.quote: The proposal of this thesis is to study the words of a tonal language, not in isolation, but inside texts where they acquire their real meanings/senses. This way, based on short narratives, this thesis presents some of the properties of the melodic patterns of words of the Ticuna language, spoken by the indigenous communities living in the High Solimões, in the state of Amazonas, Brazil.

tone_statements.citation: Fagua Rincón, Doris. 2004. Diagnóstico sociolingüístico del departamento del Amazonas, Los Lagos (periferia de Leticia): contacto y cambio. Bogotá: Universidad Nacional de Colombia. [Cap. 8 = Anexo 3: Notas sobre la fonología y la morfosintaxis de la lengua ticuna]
tone_statements.quote: En el plano fonético existe un sistema tonal de cinco niveles que corresponden a las realizaciones de los tonemas alto, medio y bajo. Las alturas tonales permiten distinguir pares mínimos y se asocian a ciertos morfemas gramaticales … No hay olvidar que la unidad fonológica que lleva el tono es la sílaba, por tal razón a cada sílaba corresponde un fonema. Esta lengua presenta tonos modulados y la variedad de alturas describe terrazas tonales, fenómeno característico de la realización de superficie de esta lengua.
tone_statements.translation: At the phonetic level there is a five-level tonal system corresponding to the realisations of the high, mid and low tonemes. The pitch heights distinguish minimal pairs and are associated with certain grammatical morphemes … It must not be forgotten that the phonological unit that bears tone is the syllable, so one [tone] phoneme corresponds to each syllable. This language has modulated [contour] tones and the range of heights describes tonal terraces, a phenomenon characteristic of this language's surface realisation.
tone_statements.locator: p. 123, section 1.3 'El tono'; tone orthography and word-level tonal schemes p. 124
tone_statements.summary: Three tonemes (high, mid, low) on five phonetic levels; the syllable bears tone; six tonal schemes for monomorphemic words; surface contours and terracing; summary after Montes 1995.

sources.quote: 1. A sílaba mais à esquerda de uma raiz é portadora de acento. 2. Os parâmetros da linha 0 são [+ cabeça terminal, + limitado], dominância à esquerda, construção do constituinte da direita para a esquerda; (esses parâmetros se aplicam utilizando-se a duração e/ou a altura). [...] A primeira regra, por exemplo, faz de uma sílaba mais à esquerda da raiz uma sílaba acentuada. Como a grande maioria das raízes em Tikuna é de dissílabos, a sílaba mais à esquerda da raiz acaba sendo a penúltima. [Translation: 1. The leftmost syllable of a root bears stress. 2. Line-0 parameters are [+terminal head, +bounded], left dominance, constituent construction right-to-left (applied using duration and/or pitch). ... The first rule makes the leftmost syllable of the root a stressed syllable. Since the great majority of Tikuna roots are disyllabic, the leftmost syllable of the root ends up being the penult.] (pp. 607, 616)
sources.note: Vol. II p.607 (PDF 872): rule '1. A sílaba mais à esquerda de uma raiz é portadora de acento'; pp.615-616 (PDF 880-881): stress realized as long duration on leftmost root syllable; since most roots are disyllabic it usually ends up penultimate, antepenultimate in compounds; content monosyllables long/stressed; metrical constituents built right-to-left below that.

sources.quote: Duração: De acordo com Soares (1992a), a duração longa do núcleo silábico constituído por segmento vocálico deve ser derivada por regra. Em (24), há exemplos de duração longa obtida mediante uma regra que faz da sílaba mais à esquerda de uma raiz a portadora do acento, sendo o acento interpretado como duração longa. [Translation: Duration: According to Soares (1992a), the long duration of a syllable nucleus consisting of a vowel segment must be derived by rule. In (24) there are examples of long duration obtained by a rule that makes the leftmost syllable of a root the bearer of stress, stress being interpreted as long duration.]
sources.note: The paper is mainly about tone association and the OCP (tonal dissimilation/fusion) in Tikuna, with data from four Tikuna villages in Brazil, but its section on duration states the stress rule explicitly: long vowel duration is derived by a rule that makes the leftmost syllable of a root the bearer of stress, stress being interpreted (realised) as long duration (p. 21, citing Soares 1992a). The remainder of that section (pp. 21-23) treats binary right-to-left foot construction (moraic trochees per Hayes 1991) over the duration and pitch planes. Esta lengua presenta tonos modulados y la variedad de alturas describe terrazas tonales, fenómeno característico de la realización de superficie de esta lengua.
tone.locator: p. 123, section 1.3 'El tono'; tone orthography and word-level tonal schemes p. 124
tone.translation: At the phonetic level there is a five-level tonal system corresponding to the realisations of the high, mid and low tonemes. The pitch heights distinguish minimal pairs and are associated with certain grammatical morphemes … It must not be forgotten that the phonological unit that bears tone is the syllable, so one [tone] phoneme corresponds to each syllable. This language has modulated [contour] tones and the range of heights describes tonal terraces, a phenomenon characteristic of this language's surface realisation.
tone.summary: Three tonemes (high, mid, low) on five phonetic levels; the syllable bears tone; six tonal schemes for monomorphemic words; surface contours and terracing; summary after Montes 1995.
tone.says: Three tonemes (high, mid, low) on five phonetic levels; the syllable bears tone; six tonal schemes for monomorphemic words; surface contours and terracing; summary after Montes 1995.

sources.quote: Para este objetivo, nesta investigação, seguiremos a análise de Montes (1995). No seu estudo, a autora explica que o tom fonológico apresenta três níveis de alturas possíveis, com presença de alofonias gerando cinco níveis de alturas fonéticas. O tikuna, portanto, é uma língua tonal enquanto o português não é. … quando os itens lexicais provenientes do PB entram no tikuna , recebem um contorno tonal, que será sempre médio (M), médio (M), baixo (B), o que no final das contas gera uma nova gramática, uma vez que nas palavras originais tikuna, qual tom ocorre em cada sílaba é imprevisível.

tone.translation: For this purpose, in this investigation, we follow the analysis of Montes (1995). In her study the author explains that phonological tone has three possible pitch levels, with allophony producing five phonetic pitch levels. Tikuna is therefore a tone language whereas Portuguese is not. … when lexical items from Brazilian Portuguese enter Tikuna, they receive a tonal contour which is always mid (M), mid (M), low (B), which in the end creates a new grammar, since in native Tikuna words which tone occurs on each syllable is unpredictable.
tone.summary: Tone language: after Montes (1995), three phonological levels (high, mid, low), five phonetic by allophony; native tone unpredictable per syllable; Portuguese loans take a fixed M..M-L contour.
tone.says: Tone language: after Montes (1995), three phonological levels (high, mid, low), five phonetic by allophony; native tone unpredictable per syllable; Portuguese loans take a fixed M..M-L contour.

sources.citation: Felix, Nazareno Sampaio. 2018. Do texto à melodia das palavras na língua Ticuna. Dissertação (Mestrado Profissional em Linguística e Línguas Indígenas), Museu Nacional, Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro, Rio de Janeiro.
sources.quote: The proposal of this thesis is to study the words of a tonal language, not in isolation, but inside texts where they acquire their real meanings/senses. This way, based on short narratives, this thesis presents some of the properties of the melodic patterns of words of the Ticuna language, spoken by the indigenous communities living in the High Solimões, in the state of Amazonas, Brazil.
sources.note: 'The proposal of this thesis is to study the words of a tonal language.. this thesis presents some of the properties of the melodic patterns of words of the Ticuna language, spoken by the indigenous communities living in the High Solimões'; word entries are given 'together with their melodies and uses in sentences.. presented in paradigms', aiming to refine Soares's (2000a,b) Ticuna dictionary and 'the spread of the knowledge of a tonal language'. Inventory not stated in the abstract.
